newsitem.title: SWEDEN: FOCUS - Swedish bank merger idea highlights problems.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Swedish bank merger idea highlights problems.

text.p: A possible merger between Sweden's two largest commercial banks, S-E-Banken and Handelsbanken, is an intriguing idea but hardly realistic, banking analysts said on Monday.
Swedish business daily Dagens Industri (DI) reported at the weekend that the two banks had entered into "tentative" merger talks in recent weeks which would create a Nordic banking giant.
Both banks declined to comment on the article, which was based on the comments of an unidentified source.

Even so, shares in the two banks moved ahead strongly in an otherwise weak bourse on Monday as the market digested the news. At 1100 GMT S-E-Banken was 1.50 crowns higher at 60.50 crowns and Handelsbanken was up 4.5 at 159 crowns.

"He (DI's reporter) is probably right that the two managements have been talking to each other, but from there it's a long way to a full-blown merger. There are some massive obstacles," one banking analyst said.
The appeal of a merger is evident. The two banks have a combined total of 732 branch offices in Sweden, and analysts said around a third of these could ultimately be axed.

This would mean considerable potential for cost-cutting in an industry that is already extremely cost-efficient in an international perspective. With lending margins under pressure, this would be a welcome route to higher profits.

Not only that, the volume advantages would be considerable. The two banks command 40 percent of the Swedish lending market, and Handelsbanken in particular has substantial interests in other Nordic countries.
However, size could prove to be a disadvantage, one Swedish banking analyst said.
"A market share of 40 percent is pretty difficult to defend. This is a classic case of the whole being less than the sum of its parts," he said.

But anlaysts said the main hurdle to the creation of a Nordic banking giant with a combined balance sheet total of over 1,100 billion crowns ($166 billion) would be an unusually severe clash in the corporate cultures of the two banks.

S-E-Banken falls firmly within the domain of Sweden's mighty Wallenberg dynasty, which controls or exerts a powerful influence in companies ranging from telecoms giant Ericsson to investment group Investor, which in turn controls a sizeable proportion of Swedish industry.
Handelsbanken in turn has its own "sphere", which incorporates forestry group MoDo and industrial holding company Industrivarden.
Merging the two banks would turn the structure of Swedish business and industry upside down, and the problems would not end there.

Handelsbanken's traditionally conservative, cost-conscious approach to banking and its decentralised structure would be hard to marry with S-E-Banken's more adventurous but highly centralised structure.

Then there is the problem of ownership. Initially, Handelsbanken would account for around 60 percent of the equity capital of the new bank, but S-E-Banken would hardly be willing to enter an alliance on unequal terms.
Add the frictions caused as thousands of employees are made redundant and a probably sceptical attitude from competition authorities, and the attraction of a merger recedes further.
In fact, there is at least one strong indication the problem will never arise.
The Stockholm Stock Exchange, which has right of access to any information that could potentially move share prices, said it would not act on the report.
"We have received such information and we see no reason to take any measures," spokesman Hans Edenhammar said. ($1=6.61 crowns)
